::: {.puzzle}
A kalimba tine's first [overtone](glossary.qmd#partial) sits at about 6.3 times its [fundamental](glossary.qmd#fundamental), nowhere near a whole number. Overtones off the whole numbers are what make a bell clang. So why does a kalimba sound like a clean note?
:::

Tap a tine. Then tick the box that keeps the overtones ringing, and tap it again.

::: {.gist}
**The gist.** The overtones really are off the whole numbers, and you do hear them, as the brief metallic click at the start of each note. But they die within a fraction of a second, while the fundamental rings on. The fundamental, left ringing on its own, is a clean note. Tick the box to keep the overtones ringing, and the same tine clangs like a bell.
:::

## On the pitch ruler

Here are one tine's frequencies: 1×, then 6.27×, far from the gray whole-number lines, and further up 17.55× and 34.39×, off the right edge. Each stem's height is how hard that mode [pushes sideways](glossary.qmd#moment) on the bridge just after a pluck, one of the two loads a tine puts on the bridge (the fold at the end has both). Tap a stem to see the shape of that mode.

```{=html}
<div class="ins">

    <h3>Modes of one tine · tap a stem</h3>
    <svg class="spec" id="kSpec" viewBox="0 0 320 120" aria-label="Partials of a plucked tine"></svg>
    <canvas id="kShape" style="height:140px" aria-label="Side view of the selected tine mode"></canvas>

  </div>
</div>
```

## How it works

**A tine resists bending.** A string is held straight by tension. A tine is under no tension at all: it springs back because steel resists being bent. That one change, bending instead of stretching, is behind both of the tine's surprises below, through one fact: squeeze a shape into half the length, and a string pulls it back 4 times harder, but a tine pushes it back 16 times harder. Why 4 and 16? Squeezing a shape into half the length doubles every rate of change along it. A string's pull depends on its bending, a rate of change of a rate of change: 2 × 2 = 4. A tine's push depends on how that bending itself changes along the tine, twice over: 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16. (In the equation of motion, four derivatives where the string had two; the fold has the details.)

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Step-by-step derivation</span>The tine's equation: four derivatives instead of two <span class="needs">uses partial derivatives and integrals over an area</span></summary>

Let $u(x, t)$ be the tine's height at distance $x$ from the clamp at time $t$; subscripts are [partial derivatives](glossary.qmd#partial-derivative). A tine of [Young's modulus](glossary.qmd#youngs-modulus) $E$ (how stiff the steel is), cross-section area $S$, [second moment of area](glossary.qmd#second-moment) $I$ (how the cross-section's shape resists bending) and density $\rho$ obeys the [Euler–Bernoulli beam](glossary.qmd#beam) equation
$$
u_{tt} = -\kappa^2\,u_{xxxx}, \qquad \kappa^2 = \frac{EI}{\rho S}.
$$
Its operator is $\kappa^2\,d^4/dx^4$, where the string's was $-c^2\,d^2/dx^2$. Two of the four derivatives measure how sharply the tine is bent, its curvature $u_{xx}$; the steel answers with a turning effect, the *bending moment*, proportional to it. One more turns the change of bending moment along the tine into the sideways force across each cut, the *shear force*, and the last turns the change of shear force along the tine into the net force on each piece.

**Why $1/L^2$.** Take a tine twice as long, with the same cross-section; its mode shapes stretch to twice the length. Each of the four derivatives along the tine is then half as large, so the restoring force on the same shape is $2^4 = 16$ times weaker, while the mass per unit length is unchanged. Frequency goes as the square root of force over mass, so it drops by a factor of 4: frequency goes as $1/L^2$. For a string, two derivatives give $2^2 = 4$ and a factor of 2: frequency as $1/L$.

The derivation, step by step:

```{=html}
<div class="ins">
<div class="panel">
    <svg class="slice" viewBox="0 0 320 170" role="img" aria-label="A slice of the tine with bending moments and shear forces on both faces">
      <line class="ax" x1="20" y1="85" x2="300" y2="85"/>
      <rect class="bar" x="110" y="65" width="100" height="40" rx="2"/>
      <path class="m" d="M 96 55 A 32 32 0 0 0 96 115"/><path class="mh" d="M 90 113 L 100 120 L 101 109 Z"/>
      <path class="m" d="M 224 55 A 32 32 0 0 1 224 115"/><path class="mh" d="M 230 113 L 220 120 L 219 109 Z"/>
      <line class="v" x1="110" y1="85" x2="110" y2="140"/><path class="vh" d="M 104 136 L 116 136 L 110 148 Z"/>
      <line class="v" x1="210" y1="85" x2="210" y2="30"/><path class="vh" d="M 204 34 L 216 34 L 210 22 Z"/>
      <text x="58" y="88">M</text><text x="248" y="88">M + dM</text>
      <text x="118" y="150">V</text><text x="218" y="30">V + dV</text>
      <text x="146" y="128">dx</text>
    </svg>
    <p class="cap">One slice of the tine. Bending moments (warm), the turning effects that bend it; shear forces (cool), the sideways forces across each cut, push it up and down. Torque balance links them; force balance moves the slice.</p>
  </div>
</div>
```

**1. Bending stresses.** Bend the bar. Fibers on the outside of the curve stretch and fibers on the inside compress, while a middle line, the *neutral axis*, keeps its length.

```{=html}
<svg class="fig" viewBox="0 0 420 150" role="img" aria-label="A bent section of bar: fibers on the outside stretch, fibers on the inside compress, the middle keeps its length">
  <path class="bar" d="M 50 60 Q 210 10 370 60 L 370 100 Q 210 50 50 100 Z"/>
  <path class="dash" d="M 50 80 Q 210 30 370 80"/>
  <path class="pos" d="M 150 40 L 120 47"/><path class="pos" d="M 270 40 L 300 47"/>
  <path class="neg" d="M 140 78 L 165 72"/><path class="neg" d="M 280 78 L 255 72"/>
  <text x="168" y="22">stretched (y &gt; 0)</text><text x="160" y="118">compressed (y &lt; 0)</text>
  <text x="300" y="138">neutral axis, y = 0</text>
</svg>
```

A fiber at height $y$ above the neutral axis is stretched by the fraction $-y\,u_{xx}$ (for a gentle bend, the fraction by which a fiber stretches is its distance from the neutral axis times how fast the bar turns per unit length, which is the curvature $u_{xx}$), and by Hooke's law it carries the stress (force per area) $\sigma = -E\,y\,u_{xx}$. Summed over the cross-section these forces cancel, which is what places the neutral axis through the middle (the centroid) of the cross-section, but their torques do not. They add up to the *bending moment*
$$
M = -\int_S y\,\sigma\,dA = E\,u_{xx}\int_S y^2\,dA = EI\,u_{xx}, \qquad I = \int_S y^2\,dA ,
$$
the integrals running over the cross-section. For a rectangle of width $w$ and thickness $h$, $I = wh^3/12$; for a round wire of diameter $d$, $I = \pi d^4/64$.

**2. Shear.** A moment rotates a slice but cannot lift it. Each face of a slice also carries a vertical force, the *shear force*. The conventions: $M$ is the moment on a face that bends the slice into an upward curve, counterclockwise on the right face and clockwise on the left; $V$ is the upward force on the right face, and the left face feels the same force downward.

```{=html}
<svg class="fig" viewBox="0 0 420 170" role="img" aria-label="A thin slice with bending moments, clockwise on the left face and counterclockwise on the right face, and shear forces, down on the left face and up on the right face">
  <path class="dash" d="M 30 85 L 390 85"/>
  <rect class="bar" x="150" y="65" width="120" height="40" rx="2"/>
  <path class="pos" d="M 136 55 A 32 32 0 0 0 136 115"/><path class="fillpos" d="M 143 55 L 132 49 L 132 61 Z"/>
  <path class="pos" d="M 284 55 A 32 32 0 0 1 284 115"/><path class="fillpos" d="M 277 55 L 288 49 L 288 61 Z"/>
  <path class="neg" d="M 150 85 L 150 140"/><path class="fillneg" d="M 144 136 L 156 136 L 150 148 Z"/>
  <path class="neg" d="M 270 85 L 270 30"/><path class="fillneg" d="M 264 34 L 276 34 L 270 22 Z"/>
  <text x="96" y="90">M</text><text x="306" y="90">M + dM</text>
  <text x="158" y="152">V</text><text x="278" y="30">V + dV</text><text x="198" y="128">dx</text>
</svg>
```

We neglect the slice's resistance to being spun, its rotational inertia, which is accurate when the bar is thin compared with the length of its bending waves; then the torques on the slice must balance. Taking torques about the left face, the shear on the right face times the lever arm $dx$ cancels the change in moment: $V\,dx + dM = 0$, so $V = -M_x$.

**3. Newton's law.** The vertical forces on the slice do not balance: $V(x + dx) - V(x) = V_x\,dx$ accelerates its mass $\rho S\,dx$. So $\rho S\,u_{tt} = V_x = -M_{xx} = -EI\,u_{xxxx}$, the equation above.

**What was assumed.** Small slopes, a uniform bar, no rotational inertia of the slices (Rayleigh's correction for it adds a small term that matters only for thick bars and high modes), and no shear deformation of the slices (Timoshenko's correction).

</details>
:::

**Half the length, two octaves up.** A string half as long sounds an octave higher. A tine half as long sounds two octaves higher: its push-back grows 16 times instead of 4, and frequency goes as the square root of the push-back (page 1), so it rises 4 times instead of 2. A tine's frequency goes as one over its length squared. That is why the low tines in the demo are not twice as long as the high ones an octave up. Kalimba makers tune a tine by sliding it over the bridge to change its free length (Kalimba Magic), and this makes a small slide go a long way.

**Overtones off the lines.** The same fact spreads the overtones out. Higher modes bend in shorter humps, and for a tine, shorter humps push back much harder, so the frequencies grow like the square of the mode number instead of the number itself. Where exactly they land depends on how the tine is held. Pinned at both ends, they would be 1, 4, 9, 16: whole numbers. Clamped at one end and free at the other, as a tine is, they are 1, 6.27, 17.55, …: off the whole numbers.

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Step-by-step derivation</span>Where 1 : 6.27 : 17.55 comes from: the four end conditions <span class="needs">uses hyperbolic functions, a 2×2 determinant and integration by parts</span></summary>

**Boundary conditions.** The bending moment is $EI\,u_{xx}$ and the shear force is $-EI\,u_{xxx}$ (the fold above derives both). At the base the tine is held down, so it can neither move nor tilt: $u = 0$ and $u_x = 0$. A bar held this way at one end and free at the other is called a [cantilever](glossary.qmd#cantilever). At the free tip nothing pushes or bends the bar, so both the moment and the shear force vanish: $u_{xx} = 0$ and $u_{xxx} = 0$. That is two conditions at each end, four in all.

**Spectrum.** Substituting a mode $X(x)\cos\omega t$ into the equation gives $\kappa^2 X'''' = \omega^2 X$. Write $\omega/\kappa = \beta^2$, so that $X'''' = \beta^4 X$; the number $\beta$ plays the role of the string's [wavenumber](glossary.qmd#wavenumber). Four functions solve this equation: $\cos\beta x$, $\sin\beta x$, $\cosh\beta x$ and $\sinh\beta x$, where $\cosh y = (e^y + e^{-y})/2$ and $\sinh y = (e^y - e^{-y})/2$ are the [hyperbolic functions](glossary.qmd#hyperbolic). So $X$ is a combination of the four with four unknown constants. The four boundary conditions are four equations for those constants, and they have a solution other than all zeros exactly when
$$
\cos\beta L\,\cosh\beta L = -1 .
$$
The roots are $\beta L = 1.8751,\ 4.6941,\ 7.8548,\ 10.9955, \dots$, close to $(n - \tfrac12)\pi$ from the second one on. Since $\omega \propto \beta^2$, the frequency ratios are $1 : 6.27 : 17.55 : 34.39 : \cdots$, growing like $(2n-1)^2$. With *pinned* ends, held in place but free to pivot, so $u = u_{xx} = 0$ at both ends, the shapes $\sin(n\pi x/L)$ satisfy the conditions, four derivatives multiply them by $(n\pi/L)^4$, and the ratios are $1 : 4 : 9 : 16$. The later roots sit near $(n - \tfrac12)\pi$; if all of them did, the ratios would be the whole numbers $1 : 9 : 25$. The clamp and the free tip shift the first root most: it is $1.8751$, not $\pi/2 \approx 1.571$.

**Deriving the condition.**

1. *Clamped base.* $X(0) = 0$ and $X'(0) = 0$ leave $X = a\,(\cos\beta x - \cosh\beta x) + b\,(\sin\beta x - \sinh\beta x)$.
2. *Free tip.* Differentiating, and dropping the common factors $\beta^2$ and $\beta^3$, the conditions $X''(L) = 0$ and $X'''(L) = 0$ read, with the shorthand $C_1 = \cos\beta L$, $S_1 = \sin\beta L$, $C_2 = \cosh\beta L$, $S_2 = \sinh\beta L$:
$$
-(C_1 + C_2)\,a - (S_1 + S_2)\,b = 0, \qquad (S_1 - S_2)\,a - (C_1 + C_2)\,b = 0 .
$$
3. *Nonzero solution.* Two equations $pa + qb = 0$ and $ra + sb = 0$ have a solution other than $a = b = 0$ exactly when $ps - qr = 0$, the *determinant*: solve the first for $a$ and substitute into the second. Here
$$
(C_1 + C_2)^2 + (S_1 + S_2)(S_1 - S_2) = C_1^2 + S_1^2 + 2C_1C_2 + C_2^2 - S_2^2 = 2 + 2C_1C_2 = 0,
$$
using $C_1^2 + S_1^2 = 1$ and $C_2^2 - S_2^2 = 1$. So $\cos\beta L\cosh\beta L = -1$.
4. *Roots.* Since $\cosh\beta L$ grows fast, $\cos\beta L$ must be close to 0, so $\beta L \approx (n - \tfrac12)\pi$, and the approximation improves quickly with $n$. The first root, $1.8751$, is the furthest from it.

The operator $d^4/dx^4$ with these four conditions is symmetric, by integrating by parts four times (the boundary terms all vanish), so its eigenvalues are real and its eigenfunctions perpendicular, as on the circle; with the right domain it is also self-adjoint. Integrating by parts twice gives $\int_0^L X\,X''''\,dx = \int_0^L (X'')^2\,dx$, so no eigenvalue is negative, and zero is ruled out because $X'' = 0$ with a clamped base forces $X = 0$. That is why $\beta$ is a real, positive number.

</details>
:::

**Why the note still sounds clean.** You might guess the overtone is too quiet to hear. It isn't. In how far the tine swings, the overtone is tiny; but the body hears the push on the bridge, not the swing, and in that push the overtone starts strong (fold below). That strong start is the click at the beginning of each note. What keeps the note clean is that the overtone dies within a fraction of a second, while the fundamental rings on. Why it dies so fast is not computed here; the page takes it from measurement. The acoustician D. M. F. Chapman found exactly this pattern on a real kalimba: one dominant overtone, at 5.9 to 6.8 times the fundamental, gone soon after the attack.

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Step-by-step derivation</span>How strongly a pluck at the tip excites each mode <span class="needs">uses integration by parts</span></summary>

Chapman measured the tines of one kalimba, a Hugh Tracey pentatonic, and found one dominant overtone at 5.9 to 6.8 times the fundamental, near the ideal 6.27, dying away quickly after the attack. A real tine is clamped a little behind the bridge and rests on the bridge partway along, rather than being perfectly clamped at one point, and he found that the measured ratios depend on how the bridge divides the tine's length, which is one reason they spread. The steps below compute, for the ideal tine, how much of each mode a pluck starts. In short: in displacement, the second mode starts at only 2.5% of the first; but at the clamp, where in this ideal model the tine presses on the bridge, it starts at about 16% of the first in bending moment and 55% in shear force. Those are two different measures of the push on the bridge, not a range of uncertainty.

1. *The pluck shape.* Before release, a push $F$ at the tip holds the tine still in a bent shape $u_0$, so the bar's restoring force balances the push.
2. *Split it into modes.* Write $u_0 = \sum_n c_n X_n$, with each mode scaled so that $\int_0^L X_n^2\,dx = L$. Inside the tine nothing pushes, so $EI\,u_0'''' = 0$ there; the push enters only at the tip, as the shear force there. Now compute $\int_0^L EI\,u_0\,X_n''''\,dx$ in two ways. First, $EI\,X_n'''' = \rho S\,\omega_n^2X_n$ (the mode equation), and the modes are perpendicular, so only the $c_n$ term survives: the integral is $\rho S L\,\omega_n^2\,c_n$. Second, integrate by parts four times to move the derivatives onto $u_0$, as in the fold above. Inside, $EI\,u_0'''' = 0$; at the clamp both $u_0$ and $X_n$ vanish with their slopes; at the tip $X_n'' = X_n''' = 0$ and $u_0'' = 0$. The one term left is the tip's shear force times $X_n(L)$, which is $F\,X_n(L)$. So $\rho S L\,\omega_n^2\,c_n = F\,X_n(L)$. This is page 1's spring again: mode $n$ is a spring of stiffness proportional to $\omega_n^2$, pushed with a force proportional to its value at the tip, and it gives way by force over stiffness.
3. *Tip values.* Taking $a = -1$ and $b = \sigma_n$ in the fold above gives the standard form $X_n = \cosh\beta_nx - \cos\beta_nx - \sigma_n(\sinh\beta_nx - \sin\beta_nx)$, with $\sigma_n = (\sinh\beta_nL - \sin\beta_nL)/(\cosh\beta_nL + \cos\beta_nL)$, about $0.734$ and $1.018$ for the first two modes. Written this way, each mode already has $\int_0^L X_n^2\,dx = L$, and its tip value is $\pm2$ for every $n$ (a known property of clamped–free modes, easily confirmed numerically). So $c_n \propto 1/\omega_n^2$, and $c_2/c_1 = 1/6.27^2 \approx 2.5\%$.
4. *Forces.* In this model the tine is clamped right at the bridge, so the forces at the clamp are the forces on the bridge. The bending moment at the clamp is $EI\,u_{xx}$ there, and the shear force $EI\,u_{xxx}$ there (up to sign). From the standard form, $X_n''(0) = 2\beta_n^2$ and $X_n'''(0) = -2\sigma_n\beta_n^3$. Multiplying by $c_n \propto 1/\omega_n^2 \propto 1/\beta_n^4$, the second mode's moment at the clamp is $(\beta_1/\beta_2)^2 = (1.875/4.694)^2 \approx 16\%$ of the first's, and its shear force $(\sigma_2/\sigma_1)(\beta_1/\beta_2) \approx 1.39 \times 0.40 \approx 55\%$.

</details>
:::

## What we found

On the pitch ruler, a kalimba tine's frequencies are off the lines, so by the series' rule it should clang. It doesn't, because the off-line overtones die almost at once and leave one frequency ringing. Along the way, the tine taught two things: because shorter humps push back so much harder, its frequencies grow like the square of the mode number, and the way the ends are held decides whether they land on whole numbers.

::: {.family}
**Same math elsewhere.** Harmonica reeds and the steel comb of a music box are also bars held at one end and free at the other.
:::

## The next puzzle

A harmonica reed is the same kind of bar, with the same off-line overtones. Blown, though, its notes land exactly on the lines. Where did the overtones go?

<script src="core.js"></script>
<script>
(function () {
  "use strict";
  var C = Core;
  var STEPS = [0, 2, 4, 5, 7, 9, 11];
  var NOTES = [];
  for (var i = 0; i < 17; i++) { var oct = Math.floor(i / 7), key = 60 + 12 * oct + STEPS[i % 7]; NOTES.push({ key: key, f: C.mtof(key), name: C.noteName(C.mtof(key)).name }); }
  // positions: lowest in the center, then alternating left and right
  var ORDER = new Array(17), center = 8;
  for (var i = 0; i < 17; i++) { var off = Math.ceil(i / 2) * (i % 2 ? -1 : 1); ORDER[center + off] = i; }
  var longOv = false, cache = {}, plucks = {};
  var cv = document.getElementById("kal"), ctx = cv.getContext("2d");
  function geom() {
    var d = C.fit(cv), W = cv.width, H = cv.height, slot = W / 17, yb = H - 34 * d, Lmax = yb - 28 * d;
    return { d: d, W: W, H: H, slot: slot, yb: yb, Lmax: Lmax };
  }
  function tineLen(g, n) { return g.Lmax * Math.sqrt(NOTES[0].f / NOTES[n].f); }
  function buffer(n) {
    var k = n + (longOv ? "L" : "S");
    if (!cache[k]) cache[k] = C.render(C.toHz(C.models.kalimba.partials({ f1: NOTES[n].f, longOvertones: longOv }), NOTES[n].f), longOv ? 3.2 : 2.6);
    return cache[k];
  }
  function pluck(n) {
    C.play(buffer(n), 0.8); plucks[n] = performance.now();
    var nn = NOTES[n]; document.getElementById("kRead").innerHTML = "<b>" + nn.name + "</b> · " + nn.f.toFixed(1) + " Hz · first overtone at " + (nn.f * C.KM[1].ratio).toFixed(0) + " Hz";
  }
  function hit(e) {
    var r = cv.getBoundingClientRect(), g = geom(), px = (e.clientX - r.left) * g.d, py = (e.clientY - r.top) * g.d;
    var slot = Math.max(0, Math.min(16, Math.floor(px / g.slot))), n = ORDER[slot];
    return (py < g.yb + 20 * g.d && py > g.yb - tineLen(g, n) - 16 * g.d) ? n : -1;
  }
  var down = false, lastN = -1;
  cv.addEventListener("pointerdown", function (e) { down = true; cv.setPointerCapture(e.pointerId); var n = hit(e); lastN = n; if (n >= 0) pluck(n); });
  cv.addEventListener("pointermove", function (e) { if (!down) return; var n = hit(e); if (n >= 0 && n !== lastN) pluck(n); lastN = n; });
  function up() { down = false; lastN = -1; }
  cv.addEventListener("pointerup", up); cv.addEventListener("pointercancel", up);
  document.getElementById("keq").addEventListener("change", function (e) { longOv = e.target.checked; kspec(); });

  function draw(now) {
    var g = geom(), d = g.d; ctx.clearRect(0, 0, g.W, g.H);
    ctx.fillStyle = C.rgb("--wood", 0.45); ctx.fillRect(0, g.yb - 6 * d, g.W, g.H - g.yb + 6 * d);
    ctx.font = (11 * d) + "px 'IBM Plex Mono', monospace"; ctx.textAlign = "center";
    for (var s = 0; s < 17; s++) {
      var n = ORDER[s], L = tineLen(g, n), cx = (s + 0.5) * g.slot, w = Math.min(g.slot * 0.55, 14 * d), wob = 0;
      var t0 = plucks[n];
      if (t0 != null) { var dt = (now - t0) / 1000; if (dt < 2.5) wob = 3.5 * d * Math.exp(-dt * 2.2) * Math.sin(dt * 2 * Math.PI * 9); }
      ctx.fillStyle = C.rgb(t0 != null && now - t0 < 600 ? "--accent" : "--metal");
      ctx.beginPath();
      ctx.moveTo(cx - w / 2, g.yb + 14 * d); ctx.lineTo(cx - w / 2 + wob * 0.2, g.yb - L + w / 2);
      ctx.arc(cx + wob, g.yb - L + w / 2, w / 2, Math.PI, 0); ctx.lineTo(cx + w / 2, g.yb + 14 * d); ctx.closePath(); ctx.fill();
      ctx.fillStyle = C.rgb("--muted"); ctx.fillText(NOTES[n].name.replace(/\d/, ""), cx, g.yb - L - 6 * d);
    }
    ctx.fillStyle = C.rgb("--ink"); ctx.fillRect(0, g.yb - 3 * d, g.W, 6 * d);
    drawShape(now);
    requestAnimationFrame(draw);
  }

  var sel = 0, sv = document.getElementById("kShape"), sctx = sv.getContext("2d");
  function kspec() {
    var p = C.models.kalimba.partials({ longOvertones: longOv });
    C.stems(document.getElementById("kSpec"), p, { W: 320, H: 120, rmax: 12, fs: 9, sw: 2.5, noOff: true, sel: sel, onPick: function (i) { sel = i; kspec(); tone(i); } });
    var m = C.KM[sel];
    document.getElementById("kSel").innerHTML = sel ? "mode " + (sel + 1) + " · <b>" + m.ratio.toFixed(2) + "×</b> the fundamental · " + (Math.log2(m.ratio) * 12).toFixed(1) + " semitones up" : "mode 1 · the fundamental";
  }
  function tone(i) { C.play(C.render([{ f: 440 * C.KM[i].ratio, amp: 1, tau: 0.6 }], 1.2), 0.6); }
  function drawShape(now) {
    var d = C.fit(sv), W = sv.width, H = sv.height, x0 = 22 * d, x1 = W - 14 * d, mid = H / 2, A = H * 0.36, f = C.KM[sel].shape, mx = 0;
    for (var i = 0; i <= 120; i++) mx = Math.max(mx, Math.abs(f(i / 120)));
    var ph = C.reduce ? 1 : Math.cos(2 * Math.PI * Math.min(3, 0.4 * Math.sqrt(C.KM[sel].ratio)) * now / 1000);
    sctx.clearRect(0, 0, W, H);
    sctx.strokeStyle = C.rgb("--grid"); sctx.lineWidth = d; sctx.beginPath(); sctx.moveTo(x0, mid); sctx.lineTo(x1, mid); sctx.stroke();
    sctx.fillStyle = C.rgb("--ink"); sctx.fillRect(x0 - 12 * d, mid - 26 * d, 12 * d, 52 * d);
    sctx.strokeStyle = C.rgb("--accent"); sctx.lineWidth = 3 * d; sctx.beginPath();
    for (var i = 0; i <= 160; i++) { var xi = i / 160, y = mid - A * ph * f(xi) / mx, x = x0 + xi * (x1 - x0); if (i) sctx.lineTo(x, y); else sctx.moveTo(x, y); }
    sctx.stroke();
    sctx.fillStyle = C.rgb("--ink"); var prev = f(0.01);
    for (var i = 2; i <= 160; i++) { var cur = f(i / 160); if (prev * cur < 0) { sctx.beginPath(); sctx.arc(x0 + (i - 0.5) / 160 * (x1 - x0), mid, 3.5 * d, 0, 2 * Math.PI); sctx.fill(); } prev = cur; }
  }
  C.onTheme(kspec);
  kspec(); requestAnimationFrame(draw);
})();
</script>
